standard.title: Interpretations of Medieval Europe
standard.description: interpretations about an event, individual, group, institution or movement in Medieval, Renaissance or pre-modern Europe
standard.prior_knowledge: Students explain historical interpretations about significant events, individuals and groups in ancient contexts (AC9HH7K — implicit from prior band) and have developed skills in source analysis (AC9HH7S07). They have not yet examined how and why historians construct different interpretations of the same medieval or early modern subject, including how myths, misconceptions and changing access to sources shape historical understanding.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain how and why historians have developed different interpretations about events, individuals, groups, institutions or movements in Medieval, Renaissance or pre-modern Europe — including what evidence those interpretations rest on, why they differ, and how interpretations have changed over time.

nodes.label: What is a historical interpretation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the difference between historical fact and historical interpretation, and describe why the same event or individual can be interpreted differently by different historians.
nodes.minimum_width: An explanation of the distinction between fact and interpretation applied to one medieval or early modern subject.
nodes.typical_width: The concept of historical interpretation — how historians use evidence, personal perspective, and the context in which they work to construct accounts; the distinction between myth/legend and historical evidence (e.g. King Arthur, Pope Joan) as a clear illustration of why interpretation must be grounded in evidence.
wider: Examine how historians have disproved medieval myths such as King Arthur or Pope Joan, showing how new evidence and rigorous method change interpretations

Explore how the interpretations of the Scientific Revolution or the Enlightenment have changed over time — from being seen as purely European achievements to being understood in a broader intercultural context
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish between fact and interpretation, or who treat historical accounts as simply true or false, cannot analyse competing interpretations. The conceptual distinction is necessary for all subsequent nodes.

response_modes.reason: The fact/interpretation distinction is deceptively simple — students need explicit scaffolding to understand that interpretation is not just opinion but a reasoned, evidence-based account that can be evaluated. Use concrete medieval examples (myths vs documented history) to make the distinction tangible.

success_criteria: Explains the difference between a historical fact and a historical interpretation using a specific medieval or early modern example
Identifies at least one reason why historians might interpret the same event or individual differently

nodes.label: Competing interpretations and why they differ
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe competing historical interpretations of a chosen subject and explain why historians have reached different conclusions — including differences in access to sources, personal perspective, and the historical context in which historians worked.
nodes.minimum_width: Two different interpretations of the chosen subject with at least one explanation of why they differ.
nodes.typical_width: Multiple competing interpretations analysed for their evidentiary basis and the factors that shaped them; the Black Death as misconceived as primarily a European event; contrasting perspectives on the role of women in Renaissance society; the 'Gold, God and Glory' framework for Spanish conquest as a contested interpretation.
wider: Analyse the importance of key women in Renaissance society — Caterina Sforza, Isabella d'Este, Lucrezia Borgia, Catherine de Medici — using artwork, written sources and historians' interpretations to examine how gendered assumptions shaped historical accounts
Examine why the Black Death has been misconceived as predominantly European, with reference to differing historians' interpretations and evidence from affected regions in Asia and the Middle East

response_modes.reason: The range of medieval subjects for which competing interpretations exist is wide. Using multiple subjects (Black Death, Renaissance women, Scientific Revolution) prevents students from treating interpretation as specific to one case and helps them see it as a general feature of historical knowledge.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The case of Renaissance women — whose historical significance was systematically undervalued — is rich context for showing how interpretations are shaped by power and perspective, not just evidence. This deepens students' understanding of historiography as a practice with its own history.
success_criteria: Describes at least two different historical interpretations of the chosen subject
Explains at least one reason why the interpretations differ (e.g. access to sources, perspective, historical context of the historian)

nodes.label: Evaluating interpretations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate historical interpretations by examining the evidence they rest on and identifying factors that might limit or strengthen them.
nodes.minimum_width: An evaluation of at least one interpretation using evidence to assess its strengths or limitations.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluation of competing interpretations using source evidence; how discoveries of science are linked to ideas about the free exercise of human reason; how the importance or significance of the Scientific Revolution or Enlightenment is highlighted or questioned depending on the interpretive lens used.
wider: Examine how the interpretations of the Enlightenment and Scientific Revolution highlight their importance to contemporary society, evaluating how much weight to give modern relevance as a criterion in judging historical significance

Analyse how modern historians' interpretations of the Crusades differ depending on whether they focus on European, Islamic or Byzantine perspectives — and evaluate which interpretation is best supported by the available evidence

response_modes.reason: Students need a method for evaluating interpretations — not just noting that they differ but asking which is better supported, by what evidence, and why. Scaffold the evaluation process explicitly: identify the claim, identify the evidence, assess the strength of the link.

success_criteria: Evaluates at least one historical interpretation by identifying evidence that supports or limits it
Explains how factors such as source availability, perspective or historical context affect the strength of an interpretation
